passages.t: On Mount Moriah: the foundation and the main hall
passages.happening: ‘Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to his father David. This was the place that David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite’ (verse 1). He begins in the second month of the fourth year of his reign (verse 2). The foundation is sixty cubits by twenty, ‘according to the old standard’ (verse 3). The portico, the main hall and its beams, walls and doors are overlaid with gold, ‘He adorned the temple with precious stones for beauty, and its gold was from Parvaim’ (verse 6), and cherubim are carved on the walls (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
With labor and materials ready, building begins. This chapter and the next are the Chronicler's inventory of the temple, and they complete a line that began when David bought Ornan's threshing floor to stop the plague and named it the place for God's house. They also complete the move from the tabernacle, the tent of the wilderness, to a house that stays.

The name Moriah appears only twice in the Old Testament: here and in Genesis 22, where God sends Abraham to the land of Moriah to offer Isaac. The Chronicler is the only biblical writer to make the connection. The place where Abraham's son was spared and the place where David's plague was stopped become the place of the temple.

First Kings 6:1 gives the same year and dates it 480 years after the exodus, which places it around 966 BC on the common reckoning, a figure that is also part of the debate over the date of the exodus. Kings says the building took seven years. The old standard cubit was probably an older, longer royal cubit of about 52 centimeters, a little over twenty inches, rather than the common cubit of about 45. Parvaim, the source of the gold, is not known from any other source.

The plan, a long building entered through a porch, with a main hall and an inner room at the back, belongs to a type known from the Levant and northern Syria. Excavated temples at Ain Dara in Syria and Tell Tayinat in southern Turkey have a similar three-part layout from about the same era. No remains of Solomon's temple have been identified, but its design fit its world.
passages.later: Genesis says that God told Abraham to ‘go to the land of Moriah’ (Genesis 22:2). First Kings dates the start: ‘In the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt’ (1 Kings 6:1).
passages.asks: The temple was built where a father was spared his son and a king was spared his people. Ask what places in your own life have become holy because mercy met you there. And ask what you would build on them.

passages.t: The Most Holy Place, the veil, and two pillars
passages.happening:
‘Then he made the Most Holy Place’ (verse 8), twenty cubits each way, overlaid with six hundred talents of fine gold. ‘In the Most Holy Place he made two cherubim of sculptured work, and he overlaid them with gold’ (verse 10); their wings reach from wall to wall (verses 11-13). ‘He made the veil of blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, with cherubim woven into it’ (verse 14).

In front of the temple stand two pillars with capitals, chains and a hundred pomegranates (verses 15-16). ‘The pillar on the south he named Jachin, and the pillar on the north he named Boaz’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Ancient temples were built as earthly homes for a god, and their decoration often pictured a garden of abundance. Solomon's temple follows the pattern: palm trees, chains, pomegranates and cherubim recall Eden, where cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life. Gold on every surface marked the house as royal and holy; the word gold comes nine times in the chapter.

Cherubim, keruv, were winged guardian figures, often pictured with animal bodies and human faces, who flanked thrones and guarded holy places. In the Most Holy Place two huge cherubim spread their wings from wall to wall, forming a throne above the ark. The veil, paroketh, the word used for the tabernacle's curtain, separated the inner room. Only the high priest went behind it, once a year on the Day of Atonement. Jachin probably means he establishes, and Boaz is usually understood as in him is strength, though both are debated.

Compared with 1 Kings 6 and 7, which give much more detail, the Chronicler keeps to what mattered for worship: the holy place, the cherubim, the veil and the gold. Some figures differ from Kings. First Kings 7:15 gives each pillar eighteen cubits, while verse 15 here gives thirty-five together. In verse 4 the traditional Hebrew gives the portico a height of 120 cubits, a tower six times taller than the building; the BSB, following some Greek and Syriac manuscripts, reads twenty. Kings mentions olivewood doors to the inner room, Chronicles the veil. The figures may be measured differently, with or without capitals or bases, and numbers were easily miscopied; the doors and the veil may both have existed. None of this touches the chapter's meaning, and the Chronicler, who knew Kings, did not try to harmonize them.
passages.later: When Jesus died, Matthew says, ‘At that moment the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom’ (Matthew 27:51).
passages.asks: The holiest room was closed by a veil that only one man could pass, once a year. Ask what it means to you that God is holy, and not easily approached. And ask what the torn veil in the Gospels says to you about how near he has come.
